solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Tests were designed to keep one cool (10)

indicators.note: the letters are arranged to a new design
the rearranged letters hold the next piece inside them

blocks.note: one = I, the Roman numeral, placed after STREETW

annotation.surface: Exam papers set up to stop a candidate panicking.
annotation.walkthrough: "Cool" reads as calm under exam pressure, but here it is the slangy sense of savvy and in the know.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone streetwise is cool in the sense of worldly and hard to fool.

entries.clue: Father ultimately shows anger (4)

indicators.note: take what comes at the very end of the next word

annotation.surface: A dad finally losing his temper.
annotation.walkthrough: "Ultimately" looks like it belongs with Father, as in the end he snaps, but it acts on "shows".
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, used mostly of animals: a stallion that sires foals is their father, and breeders list the sire and the dam.

entries.clue: Dream I will be held in respect (7)

indicators.note: one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: to revere is to respect deeply
I stays as it is, placed inside REVER…E

annotation.surface: Someone hoping that one day they will be admired.
annotation.walkthrough: "I will be held in respect" reads as an ambition; the "I" is simply the letter going inside.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the waking sense: a reverie is a daydream, a spell of being lost in pleasant thoughts.

entries.clue: NHS timetables ruined business (13)

indicators.note: the letters are wrecked and rebuilt

annotation.surface: Hospital schedules wrecking a company; the NHS is Britain's National Health Service.
annotation.walkthrough: The capitals make NHS look untouchable, but its three letters join the anagram like any others.
annotation.definitionFit: A business such as a shop or restaurant is an establishment.

entries.clue: Climber regularly waits at sea, wind rising (8)

indicators.note: take letters at regular intervals, every other one
in a down clue the word reads upwards

blocks.note: the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th and 9th letters of WAITS AT SEA

annotation.surface: A mountaineer or a sailor patiently waiting out the weather at sea.
annotation.walkthrough: "Climber" suggests a person on a rock face; here it is a climbing plant. The alternate letters run across three words.
annotation.definitionFit: Wisteria is a woody climbing plant with hanging purple flowers.

entries.clue: Vocally scares away e.g. animals or trainers? (5)

definitions.note: Covers the verb (a farrier shoes horses) and the noun (trainers are shoes).

indicators.note: the next part is spoken, not spelt

blocks.note: to shoo is to scare away

annotation.surface: Someone shouting to drive off animals or sports coaches.
annotation.walkthrough: "Trainers" looks like people who train animals, which fits the surface; it is the British word for sports shoes. Shoeing animals is what a blacksmith does to horses.
annotation.definitionFit: One shoes animals such as horses, and trainers are a kind of shoes.

entries.clue: Fools around in places for pampering (4)

indicators.note: the word is turned around

blocks.note: saps = fools, gullible people; this word is the one turned around

annotation.surface: Idiots messing about at a health resort.
annotation.walkthrough: "Fools around" reads as a single verb phrase, messing about; split it into noun and turning instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Spas are resorts where people go to be pampered.

entries.clue: Quietly put down writing instrument – small child here? (7)

blocks.note: to lay is to put down

annotation.surface: Softly setting down a pen, with a toddler nearby.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is a hint rather than a synonym, flagged by the question mark: a playpen is where a small child is kept.
annotation.definitionFit: A playpen is an enclosure where a small child is put to play safely.

entries.clue: Laugh about a young man dressing (5,5)

indicators.note: one word goes about, around, the others

blocks.note: a scream is a huge laugh, as in "it was a scream"
a lad = a young man; A LAD goes inside S…CREAM

annotation.surface: Someone laughing at a young man getting dressed.
annotation.walkthrough: "Dressing" pretends to be putting on clothes; it is the salad sort.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this is one kind of dressing, a sharp, pourable British relative of mayonnaise.

entries.clue: Fix components of motor I’ve tested (5)

indicators.note: the answer is made of parts of the following words

annotation.surface: A mechanic reporting on engine parts they have checked.
annotation.walkthrough: The mechanical surface makes "components" look like engine parts, which hides the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: To rivet is to fix something firmly, as with metal pins.

entries.clue: Deficit the result of brief American season (9)

annotation.surface: A financial gap blamed on a short American autumn.
annotation.walkthrough: "American" is there because only in American English is the season called fall; British English says autumn.
annotation.definitionFit: A shortfall is a deficit, an amount by which something falls short.

entries.clue: Dish, one hotel had it prepared (4-2-3-4)

indicators.note: the letters are made ready in a new form, as food is

annotation.surface: A menu note that a hotel had cooked a certain dish.
annotation.walkthrough: "One" looks like a number to convert to I, but here it is spelt out as part of the fodder. Toad-in-the-hole is a British dish of sausages baked in batter.
annotation.definitionFit: Toad-in-the-hole is a dish of sausages cooked in Yorkshire pudding batter.

entries.clue: Smooth unusually bad tempers having been automatically approved (6-7)

indicators.note: the letters appear in an unusual order

annotation.surface: Calming someone's unusually foul moods before something gets signed off.
annotation.walkthrough: "Bad" looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder; "unusually" is the indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: Something rubber-stamped has been approved as a formality, without real scrutiny.

entries.clue: Man getting the sack, the present supremo? (5,5)

definitions.text: Man getting the sack, the present supremo?

blocks.note: the surface reading is a man being fired; the meant reading is a man handed a big bag to carry
the surface reading is the current boss; the meant reading is the one in charge of gifts

annotation.surface: The current boss being fired.
annotation.walkthrough: "Getting the sack" means being fired, and "present" means current, so the clue reads as office politics; the sack is his bag of gifts and the presents are Christmas ones.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic definition: both halves describe the Christmas gift-bringer once "sack" and "present" take their literal senses.

entries.clue: Drunk pirate providing drink (8)

indicators.note: the letters stagger into a new order

blocks.note: providing = if, as in "providing it rains"

annotation.surface: A tipsy buccaneer handing out rum.
annotation.walkthrough: "Providing" reads as supplying; it is the conditional sense, if.
annotation.definitionFit: An aperitif is an alcoholic drink taken before a meal.

entries.clue: Engage troops for fellow from Rome? (6)

blocks.note: to sign someone is to engage them, as a club signs a player
OR = other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

annotation.surface: Hiring soldiers on behalf of a Roman man.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark covers the definition by example: any Italian man, not only a Roman, is a signor.
annotation.definitionFit: Signor is the Italian for Mr, a title for a man.

entries.clue: Empty, set off – pigs in these? (8)

indicators.note: the letters have gone off, gone bad

annotation.surface: Clearing out a space and heading off, with pigs somehow involved.
annotation.walkthrough: "Set off" reads as departing; it is the word SET plus an anagram signal. Pigs in blankets are a British Christmas side of small sausages wrapped in bacon.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by allusion to a dish: the sausages are the pigs and the bacon wrapped round them plays the bedding.

entries.clue: Note circulating that hurt? You got me! (6)

indicators.note: the note goes round the next piece

blocks.note: te is a note of the sol-fa scale
what you say when something hurts; it sits inside T…E

annotation.surface: Someone conceding a painful point in an argument.
annotation.walkthrough: "That hurt?" is the exclamation OUCH, not a question about pain.
annotation.definitionFit: Touché, from fencing, concedes that an opponent has scored a fair point.

entries.clue: Country with bad weather: finally, locate another (7)

indicators.note: take the last letter of the next word

annotation.surface: Someone fleeing a rainy country to find another one.
annotation.walkthrough: "Country" looks like the definition, but it gives UK; the definition is "another", meaning another country.
annotation.definitionFit: Ukraine is another country, following on from the UK in the wordplay.

entries.clue: “Heap” and “lot” possibly about right – for this? (8)

definitions.text: “Heap” and “lot” possibly about right – for this?

indicators.note: the letters are a possible arrangement
the rearranged letters go about the next piece

annotation.surface: Asking whether "heap" and "lot" are roughly the right words for something.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: heap and lot are words for a plethora, and the wordplay is built from them.
annotation.definitionFit: A plethora is a large amount, which heap and lot both mean.

entries.clue: Busy, about to get £200 in Monopoly? (2,3,2)

blocks.note: busy = constantly active, never sitting still
landing on the starting square in Monopoly collects £200

annotation.surface: A board-game player hurrying round to collect their money.
annotation.walkthrough: In Monopoly, passing or landing on the GO square pays £200, so a piece sitting on the GO square is collecting it.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone on the go is busy and constantly active.

entries.clue: Journalist’s second report redrafted to include leader of Norway (13)

indicators.note: the words are rewritten in a new order
the rewritten letters take in the next piece
take the first letter of the next word

blocks.note: the first letter of NORWAY, included in the mix

annotation.surface: A reporter rewriting a follow-up story to mention the Norwegian leader.
annotation.walkthrough: "Second" looks like it should shrink to S, but the whole word is fodder. The ’s joins definition to wordplay as "is".
annotation.definitionFit: A correspondent is a journalist who reports on a particular subject or place.

entries.clue: Great Russian ruler, favourite with our old Queen (5)

blocks.note: a teacher's pet is a favourite

annotation.surface: Comparing a tsar with a favourite British monarch.
annotation.walkthrough: "Great" looks like praise, but it is part of the name: Peter the Great.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by epithet: the tsar Peter I, who built St Petersburg, is remembered with "the Great" after his name.

entries.clue: Girl showing style, not the first (4)

indicators.note: the first letter is not wanted, so the word goes on without it

blocks.note: style = CLASS, minus its first letter C

annotation.surface: A stylish young woman who did not come first.
annotation.walkthrough: Style here is class, as in "she has real class"; "not the first" beheads it.
annotation.definitionFit: A lass is a girl, a northern British and Scottish word.

entries.clue: Come into view carrying child last of all, he thought (9)

indicators.note: one word carries the others inside it
take the last letter of the next word

blocks.note: to arise is to come into view
a tot is a small child
the last letter of ALL; TOT and L go inside ARIS…E

annotation.surface: A father appearing with a child and having the last word.
annotation.walkthrough: "He thought" reads as a narrator's aside; it is the definition, a man known for thinking.
annotation.definitionFit: Aristotle was a Greek philosopher, a thinker.

entries.clue: Love large character (5)

annotation.surface: A fondness for a big personality.
annotation.walkthrough: "Character" reads as a personality; it is a letter of the Greek alphabet.
annotation.definitionFit: Omega is a character, the last letter of the Greek alphabet.

entries.clue: Appear with spy and his boss? (4)

blocks.note: M is James Bond's boss, and Bond is a spy

annotation.surface: Turning up with a secret agent and his chief.
annotation.walkthrough: "Spy" works twice: as a verb it gives SEE, and as a noun it sets up "his boss", M in the Bond films.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of giving an impression, not of turning up: "she appears happy".

entries.clue: Rich American going after Miranda’s father (10)

indicators.note: this piece comes after the next one

blocks.note: in Shakespeare's The Tempest, Miranda is the daughter of the exiled duke

annotation.surface: A wealthy American chasing a woman's father.
annotation.walkthrough: "Rich" could be a man's name to go with Miranda, but it is the definition; the father is the magician of The Tempest.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: wealthy and flourishing, as a prosperous merchant is.
